To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
there is an increase in oxidative damage to proteins in skeletal muscles of normal aging female mice, but no increase in oxidative damage of lipids.
protein thiol oxidation does increase in aging skeletal muscles but protein oxidation is not a contributing factor in sarcopenia.

(1) There is no age-related increase in protein thol oxidation in muscles of aging female C57BL/ 6J mice; (2) There is a significant correlation between increasing protein carbonlylation and loss of muscle mass in aging female C57/BL6J mice; and (3) There is an age-related increase of lipofuscin in quadriceps limb of female C57BL6J mice.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms by which aging leads to loss of muscle mass and muscle function.
the role of oxidative stress in aging and sarcopenia.
the mechanisms that contribute to the loss of muscle mass with aging, which is known as sarcopenia.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the oxidative theory of aging is a valid explanation for the age related muscle loss in female mice.
there is an age-related increase of irreversible oxidative damage in skeletal muscle, but not in reversible oxidative damage, in aging mice.
protein thiol oxidation does change in gastrocnemiums of aging female mice but it is not the cause of muscle wasting.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there are no pervasive changes in the oxidation status of protein thiols in muscles of female C57BL/ 6J mice with age.
protein thiol oxidation does increase in skeletal muscles of mice with a genetic predisposition to sarcopenia, but does not increase in normal aging female mice.
there is a significant correlation between the increase in protein carbonylation and loss of muscle mass with aging in female mice.
The main takeaway from our work is that
protein thiol oxidation does NOT change in aging muscle.
there is no evidence for an age related increase in reversible oxidation (protein thiol oxidation) in skeletal muscles of normal aging female mice.
the oxidative damage to macomolecules is a major contributor to the age-related muscle wasting.
